lede: Knowing two numbers multiply to less than 8 tells you nothing about either. Knowing they multiply to less than zero tells you a great deal: one is positive and the other negative. That is why every one of these questions starts by moving everything to one side, and why the sketch that follows does the rest of the work.
can: Rearrange a quadratic inequality so that one side is zero.
Factorise for the critical values and sketch the curve.
Read the region off the sketch and write it with the right signs.

md: CCEA has set this question in every Unit 1 paper read, and the reports say the same thing: candidates solve the quadratic and then lose marks on the **region**. The algebra is the part you already know. The new skill is small — draw the curve, look at it, read the answer off.

caption: Below the axis is the middle: $2 < x < 5$. One double inequality, because it is one connected stretch.

title: What the statement asks for
md:
**FM1-QIN-01** — solve quadratic inequalities, which are restricted to quadratic expressions that factorise.
The Teacher Guidance recommends the graphical method and warns that you may have to form the inequality from a context first.
source: CCEA GCSE Further Mathematics specification, statement FM1-QIN-01 and its Teacher Guidance (page 7)

prompt: One tap to start. The curve $y = (x - 2)(x - 5)$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x = 2$ and at $x = $ ___
explain: A product is zero when one of its factors is zero. Those two values are the critical values, and they are where the whole method starts.

text: Zero on one side, first, always

md:
Suppose you meet $x(x + 2) \le 8$. It is tempting to say $x \le 8$ or $x + 2 \le 8$, and that step does not work.
A product tells you nothing on its own. Knowing that two numbers multiply to something **less than 8** does not pin either of them down. Knowing that they multiply to something **less than 0** does: one of them must be negative and the other positive.
That is why every one of these questions begins the same way — move everything to one side so the other side is zero.

prompt: What is the first line when solving $x^{2} + 3x \le 10$?
explain: Take 10 from both sides. Factorising before that is the error the Summer 2018 examiners said cost candidates every mark on the question.

md:
Once you have $(x - 2)(x - 5) \le 0$, the critical values are 2 and 5 and the curve is U-shaped.
Now the picture decides everything. A U-shaped curve dips **below** the axis between its two crossing points and sits **above** it on either side. So a question asking for $y < 0$ gives you the middle, and a question asking for $y > 0$ gives you the two outer pieces.

prompt: Using that sketch, for which values of $x$ is $(x - 2)(x - 5) > 0$?
explain: Above the axis is the two outside pieces, and they are separate, so they need two inequalities joined by the word or. No number is both less than 2 and greater than 5, so 'and' would describe nothing at all.

title: Not on the formula sheet
md:
With a **positive** $x^{2}$ coefficient and critical values $p < q$:
$(x - p)(x - q) < 0$ gives $p < x < q$, the region **between**.
$(x - p)(x - q) > 0$ gives $x < p$ or $x > q$, the two regions **outside**.
With $\le$ or $\ge$ the critical values themselves are included. With a **negative** $x^{2}$ coefficient every one of these swaps over.

explain: The critical values are $-6$ and 1, the curve is U-shaped, and $\le 0$ asks for on or below the axis, which is the stretch between them. The ends are included because the curve is allowed to be exactly zero.

title: Quadratic Inequalities - CCEA GCSE Further Mathematics
why: A Northern Ireland teacher taking the CCEA layout line by line, sketch included.

prompt: Which answer says the same thing as 'every $x$ strictly between $-4$ and 1'?
explain: A double inequality is read left to right, smallest first. Writing it the other way round describes no numbers at all, because nothing is greater than 1 and less than $-4$.

md:
If the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is negative the curve is an upside-down U — an n-shape — and everything reverses: it is **above** the axis between its crossing points and below on either side.
You have two safe routes. Sketch the n-shape as it really is, or multiply the whole inequality by $-1$ and **turn the inequality sign round**, which puts you back on a U-shaped curve. Choose one and stay with it.

alt: A sketch of the n-shaped curve y = 15 - 2x - x squared on x and y axes. It crosses the x-axis at the two marked points x = -5 and x = 3. The band between the two crossing points is tinted.
caption: An n-shape is positive in the middle: $15 - 2x - x^{2} > 0$ gives $-5 < x < 3$.

prompt: $15 - 2x - x^{2} > 0$ has critical values $-5$ and 3. What is the solution?
explain: The $x^{2}$ term is negative, so the curve is n-shaped and its positive part is the arch between the crossing points. Reading it as a U-shape is the error the Summer 2022 examiners described.

title: Where the marks actually go
md:
Summer 2018: candidates who did not bring the constant across solved the wrong quadratic and lost every mark; even those with the right critical values often gave the wrong range.
Summer 2019 and Summer 2024: most solved the quadratic, and the region went wrong where no sketch had been drawn.
Summer 2025: better than previous years, and the residual error was writing the critical values with no inequality signs, or with them the wrong way round.

prompt: A candidate finds the critical values $-2$ and 6 for a U-shaped curve and needs the region where the curve is below the axis. Which answer earns the mark?
explain: Below the axis is the single stretch between the crossing points. The second option describes no numbers, and the third is the boundary rather than the region; both appear in the Summer 2025 report.

title: Why the sketch is the method, not a decoration
md: The factorised form says where the curve meets the axis; only its shape says where it runs below and where above. Two critical values cut the axis into three stretches, and the sketch says which of them the inequality names.

prompt: $x$ is the width of a path in metres. The algebra gives $-4 < x < 3$. What goes on the answer line?
explain: A width has to be positive, so the negative half of the range is impossible. It cannot be zero either, or there is no path. Summer 2023 records most candidates losing this final mark.

md:
Move everything to one side, zero on the other.
Factorise for the critical values, then sketch.
Read the region off, inequality signs kept.
In a context, no negative width or count.

One question, four to six marks, in the first half, almost always with an instruction printed underneath to show every stage of your working. The marks run: rearrange to zero, factorise for the critical values, sketch, then read the region. Draw the sketch even when nothing asks you to. Stuck: if the question came from a context, ask what $x$ is before you write the answer.
